stories.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
stories.summary: Researcher finds 35,000 Grok Build apps wide open to anyone who looked for them.

sources.name: Ars Technica
sources.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
sources.text: Researcher finds 35,000 Grok Build apps wide open to anyone who looked for them. Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it. Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals. “We were shocked,” Claroc said in a Tuesday post . “The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link, and we had never been given it. Had the sales team bought a tool for this, it would have sat behind company sign-in, open only to the team. Built with AI, it went live open to anyone with the link. Claroc notified SpaceXSI of the privacy spill on Sunday. When no one responded, a Claroc official took to X to tag both Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer about the threat. At the time this post went live almost all data remained available with one notable exception: the contents from the 24 SpaceXSI apps. All of them were exposing the information on Monday evening. SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending an email with questions for this article. At the time this post went live, links for all 24 apps returned an “app not found” error. Claroc found sensitive data belonging to other Grok Build users, some working for Fortune 500 companies and a defense contractor. Some of the affected organizations and data revealed includes: Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he’s in the process of notifying companies. After speaking to the CISO of the luxury cruise company, it “pulled in their whole security team as soon as we shared the findings and are already working to contain the Grok exposure.” Link sharing for Grok Build is intended to streamline the process of developing and deploying apps. A user can input speech or text and have a working app ready for internal testing within minutes. The links are designed to give developers a way to get the app in front of authorized users quickly. The very left of the URLs contain two or more “dice words,” meaning randomly generated phrases such as “failing chassis traders,” although users can modify them. The rightmost portion of the link is grok.me. The URL for an X ads campaign plan was: https://cinder-crane-sand-frost.grok.me. The scheme is intended to prevent links from being easily guessable. When done correctly, a phrase comprising three dice words has roughly 38 bits of entropy, amounting to billions of possible combinations. The idea—sometimes called capability-based access control —is that possession of the URL serves as authorization to the resources behind it. Google has long used this technique to make URLs easy to share but hard to guess. A URL share on that platform might look like: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1BxiMVs0XRA5nFMdKvBdBZjgmUUqptlbs74OgvE2upms/edit There’s a fatal flaw in the way SpaceXSI has implemented the mechanism. Instead of being to the right of the domain—as is the case with Google links—the randomness for Grok Build links is positioned to the left of it. That allows the links to be easily enumerated using passive DNS services. These services monitor central DNS lookup servers. When a server lookup requests the IP address of a previously never-before-seen URL, the transaction is captured in a publicly searchable database. Had Grok followed Google’s approach, the links would have been invisible to passive DNS searchers. Muse, the Meta agent that CEO Mark Zuckerberg said was built from the ground up for security, recently suspended a link-sharing feature after it too was found leaking sensitive data . Aprozper said a passive DNS search returned 43,601 links ending in grok.me. Of them, more than 35,000, or nearly 95 percent, were public, meaning that clicking on the link opened the corresponding app and all data it stored. He said that tests he conducted over the past week showed that, by default, Grok sets links to “Anyone with the link.” Users have the option to change the setting to “invited users” or “only you.” A representative with Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired, said in an email that Grok Build “apps are private by default and nothing goes public unless the creator chooses to share it.” The representative said that competing coding agents from ChatGPT, Lovable, and Bolt also give users the ability to generate shareable links. Aprozper’s tests contradict the representative’s statement. In all cases, Grok Build required users to change anyone with the link to one of the other two options. The Cursor statement regarding other AI coding platforms is correct. Aprozper said that app builders, including Lovable, Bolt, and Replit, “also give each app its own web address, so the same DNS records expose them, too. However, Grok is where we found by fa

sources.title: A Grok vibe-coding agent leaked sensitive SpaceXSI data
sources.text: The way Grok handles links to apps allowed them to be exposed publicly. A flaw in SpaceXSI's Grok Build vibe-coding agent allowed sensitive data to leak from thousands of users including... SpaceXSI, security fraud firm Claroc told Ars Technica . The way Grok handles links to apps allowed them to be exposed publicly by certain types of DNS services, according to the security team. As a result, sensitive information involving employees was leaked out from a hospital group, a fire department and SpaceXSI itself. "We were shocked," the researchers wrote in a blog post . "The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link." The company called pages like that GhostShares, since they can be found and opened by people who were never given the link. Some of the material found from SpaceXSI included an onboarding plan, sales territory map of 594 strategic accounts, eight X advertising proposals, four live advertiser account boards and two copies of an X brand safety playbook. Only one of the exposed apps asked for a password. Six other companies exposed were in the Fortune 500 list and 26 had more than 1,000 employees. "By our estimate roughly two percent held material serious enough to rate high or critical," Claroc wrote. The problem was the way Grok Build created links. Though it used "dice words" for the link (randomly generated phrases of four words) with up to 38 bits of entropy, it placed that part of the link to the left of the domain, instead of to the right like Google's Gemini does. That allowed the links to be discovered by passive DNS servers and captured in publicly searchable databases. Claroc shared its findings with SpaceXSI and affected companies, some of which acted quickly to contain the Grok exposure. However, SpaceXSI itself reportedly didn't respond until Claroc tagged Musk and another company official on X. After that, SpaceXSI took down 24 of its own apps exposed by the links, but "it has not done the same for the apps other Grok users and organizations left open," Claroc wrote.

sources.name: TechRadar
sources.title: Elon Musk's Grok Build coding agent is leaking a serious amount of confidential data
sources.text: Grok Build, an AI-powered coding agent built by Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI, has been found leaking a mind-numbing amount of confidential data, thanks to an apparent misconfiguration in how the products are being published on the platform. SpaceXSI, established when SpaceX and xAI merged , has a product called Grok Build, which allows users to create web applications by simply describing what they want in a chatlike interface. Without having to write any of the code themselves, the users can have an app ready in minutes and publish it directly from the chat interface. The app gets a unique web address in the format .grok.me, where “name” usually consists of four random words. It is something of a privacy feature, to make sure people can’t just guess an app’s location easily. But according to security researchers Claroc, these addresses can be found through passive DNS services, which collect and index domain names observed in DNS traffic. In other words, anyone can find a published app even if their creator (or no one else, for that matter) ever shared a link for it. As Claroc explained in its report, the researchers did just that, identifying 43,601 addresses under grok.me. But finding someone’s app shouldn’t be a big deal, right? These apps are all password-protected, right? Well, wrong. The researchers found that almost all of the apps (35,578, or 94.7%) could be accessed without authentication. That means that whatever data they were holding and generating could be accessed with almost no trouble at all. Further investigation uncovered a major oversight - when users want to publish an app, they are offered three privacy choices: “Anyone with the link”, “Invited Users”, and “Only You”. Similar to how Google Docs does it, when you want to share a document. The problem here, according to Claroc, is that “Anyone with the link” is set as the default option, suggesting that most people building apps on Grok simply weren’t paying attention to the privacy and sharing options. But still, simply accessing an app doesn’t necessarily have to be a security disaster, right? It’s just an app, right? Well, wrong again. While most apps were “harmless” in that regard (think games, calculators, landing pages), one in ten contained sensitive or internal business information, and 2% exposed information serious enough to warrant a high, or critical severity rating. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Claroc found a hospital employee directory with more than 3,500 names, an intensive care briefing containing patient information, and a trucking company’s recruitment database listing more than 1,000 individuals. It also found an employee timesheet whose downloadable code contained 18 accounts with plaintext passwords, including administrator credentials . Even SpaceXSI was leaking its own classified information this way. The researchers found 24 open apps containing onboarding plans, employee names lists, a sales territory map of almost 600 strategic accounts and their pipeline, media plans and advertiser decks (all with budget tiers, including one for a US federal agency marked as confidential), seven campaign reports for advertisers around the world, and much, much more. The researchers found one solitary app, an archive of a streaming service’s ad measurement studies, that asked for a password. Everything else was left wide open. Claroc also tested to see if they could alter the data found in these apps and built two of their own to test the theory out. One allowed unauthenticated visitor to modify a shared contact database, while another automatically granted access to anyone signing in with a Google account (even if they weren’t part of the team). The researchers notified SpaceXSI about their findings on November 8, and within two days all SpaceXSI apps were no longer available. They are now working through the list and notifying everyone else. ➡️ Read our full guide to the best antivirus 1. Best overall: Bitdefender Total Security 2. sources.title: Claude can now join your weekly meeting to take notes and even start work for you — and that's not all, with new spreadsheet, whiteboard tools and more helping conquer the world of "Frontier Work"
sources.text: Anthropic wants Claude to help with "work at the frontier" Anthropic has unveiled a host of updates for Claude which could see the AI platform play a much more integral role in some of your most common work tasks. Among the next expansions are tools which allow Claude to join video calls as a participant, meaning it learns first-hand from your meetings and can start work immediately. Joining its existing suite of office software tools are new Whiteboards, Sheets and Data services looking to help users work and create more effectively - and new interactive connectors will now allow Claude to work inside the full versions of common workplace apps such as Adobe , Atlassian and HubSpot. "A year ago, Claude changed how developers work," Anthropic wrote in a blog post announcing the new tools. "Engineers stopped asking AI for snippets and started handing it whole tasks, which freed them to spend their time deciding what to build. For most other teams, work has stayed much the same: the email gets written a little faster, the meeting comes with a summary." "Now the frontier is moving to knowledge work, and people are starting to hand Claude whole tasks too." The most striking new addition is undoubtedly Claude Meetings, which will allow Claude to join video calls as a visible participant. Claude follows the conversation and starts on the work as people talk, taking notes, drafting plans, outlining timelines on whiteboards, answering chat questions, and utilizing connected work apps while conversations happen - and when the call ends, the notes, action items and everything Claude made are waiting in claude.ai. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Also new is Claude Whiteboards, a shared, real-time board which helps teams turn brainstorms and retrospectives into structured plans, timelines, and action items, and integrates directly into Claude Meetings, and Claude Sheets, a spreadsheet tool which allows teams to build and edit trackers and budgets collaboratively with Claude, complete with tabs, formulas, and dropdown menus. Finally, Claude Data (formerly known as Claude Dashboards) connects company data sources (such as CRMs and warehouses) to generate dashboards, data stories, and narrated videos, featuring beta capabilities like certified queries and live sharing. Alongside this, new Interactive Connectors will allow full versions of partner tools (like Adobe, Atlassian, HubSpot, Salesforce , NetSuite, and Workday) to open directly inside Claude, which can take actions directly within these apps with user approval. Connectors respect existing user permissions, and admins can utilize features like Claude auto-connect, usage controls, and Smart Reports to monitor team productivity and costs. Claude Meetings, Claude Whiteboard and Claude Sheets are all still in beta, with Claude Data and Interactive Connectors generally available now. sources.title: eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents
sources.text: Silicon Valley is promising an AI agent revolution, but retailers and service providers keep blocking them.﻿ Silicon Valley is promising an AI agent revolution, but retailers and service providers keep blocking them.﻿ eBay appears to have blocked AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, from browsing on the platform — the latest speed bump in the AI agent race. A reader tells The Verge that for several weeks he’s had his Muse agent browse and curate a daily digest of watches for sale on platforms like eBay, including a link to listings, price, shipping details, and relevant notes about condition or style. This weekend, though, Muse was unable to pull any links or details from eBay, with Muse saying it was blocked from the site. The Verge was able to re-create the experience using other search requests, and in some cases we found that Muse instead directed users to outside sites that mirrored eBay listings. Shopping is frequently invoked as one area where AI agents can augment or improve the human-driven experience. Technology companies tout the use of agents to book travel, find deals, and even purchase goods and services on behalf of humans. But AI agents are regularly getting blocked from accessing retailers’ sites , calling into question how useful they can really be. eBay previously updated its user agreement to ban the use of tools like “buy-for-me agents” and “LLM-driven bots” that place orders without human review. Until recently, though, agents like Muse were able to browse the site and pull listings for users. AI is becoming embedded throughout the platform for the discovery, personalization, and selling process, eBay spokesperson Sybille St. Arromand told The Verge in an email. St. Arromand declined to directly answer whether eBay recently imposed new limits on AI agents. “As it pertains to third-parties, we take a selective approach to how they access and interact with our marketplace. We have restricted agent access in certain cases, including unauthorized scraping and training on our data,” St. Arromand said. “We have ongoing discussions with potential partners and are evaluating ways third-party agents could help new customers discover eBay’s unmatched inventory, and our focus is on preserving the trusted end-to-end experience that buyers and sellers expect from eBay.” Retailers and service providers who’ve enthusiastically added AI features to their platforms have shown varying levels of comfort with third-party agents accessing their sites. On one end of the spectrum is Amazon, which is blocking external agents entirely from browsing or shopping. Some retailers like Target have restrictions in place that allow agents to successfully browse in some instances but get blocked in others. Shopify, meanwhile, has opened its catalog of a billion listings so that shoppers can set up their agents to purchase items on their behalf . Throwing agents into the e-commerce mix has the potential to upend how people shop online, partly because retail sites are largely assuming they’re selling to humans, with human limitations, and not swarms of bots. For example, The Verge discovered in October that someone could use Muse to effectively hold product listings hostage on The RealReal, a secondhand designer consignment site, by having an agent continually add the product to the user’s cart. The RealReal updated its bot system after The Verge ’s reporting. But as retailers tweak their sites in real time to handle bots, it remains unclear how widespread agentic commerce is. In fact, there are signs that most people are not using AI this way. Uber said it fulfilled only four rides via third-party agents in Q3 and only around 500 Uber Eats orders during the week of Halloween. DoorDash similarly said it fulfilled only “several hundred” orders placed via third-party agents. It reported 993 million total orders last quarter.

sources.title: Adobe wants you to spend less time editing and more time creating – Creative Cloud opens its doors to third-party AI agents
sources.text: Creative Cloud's most popular apps can now be controlled via your favorite AI agent Adobe has revealed plans to expand its Creative Agent across more of its flagship Creative Cloud applications, including Premiere, Lightroom and InDesign, in a bid to give AI more autonomy to handle the less creative side of creative work. Unlike generative AI, which acts upon single prompts, AI agents can handle longer and more complex, multi-step processes. The company positions the use of AI as putting creatives in the director ' s chair, enabling them to offload tasks that aren't really part of the creative workflow to AI agents to free them up more time to focus on the truly creative elements of their jobs. "The ideas, taste, style and vision that creative professionals bring to their work are what make their work stand out," Adobe Product Marketing VP Deepa Subramaniam stressed. Importantly, using AI agents doesn't make a creative's work less human. Some common use cases include applying effects across multiple clips, tracking masked subjects and adjusting colours and exposures in Premiere. Together with the expanded rollout, Adobe is also opening up the doors to third-party AI agents via MCP, starting with its most popular apps – Photoshop , Illustrator, Premiere and After Effects. Granting permission to third-party agents to directly work within these apps means users won't have to handle exports and jumping between multiple tools, but it also means things like Photoshop layers and Illustrator vectors will still be preserved. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! On-stage at the conference, Anil Chakravarthy, who is set to become Adobe's CEO effective from December 1 2026, demonstrated a third-party AI agent turning a long-form podcast into multiple social media snippets – a demo that was met with much excitement and applause from the thousands of attendees on the ground. Besides the more autonomous side of AI, Adobe hasn't completely ditched generative AI, which still plays a major part in creative workflows. Photoshop will be gaining new tools to add or adjust lighting within an existing photo. Generative restyle will also turn natural language prompts into adjustable sliders, helping to remove the traditionally steep learning curve often associated with Photoshop. Premiere also gains new GenAI upgrades, like audio enhancement tools and a generative remove functionality for removing unwanted objects from a series of video frames, while Lightroom sees additions like blemish removal and a tool to artificially open a subject's eyes – perfect for group photos where creatives would already be handling many other variables. While some general Creative Cloud features are now generally available, some more advanced tools like Lightroom Open Eyes and Premiere Generative Remove remain in beta.
